findings.title: [P1] Fold unquoted heredoc continuations before locating the terminator
findings.body:
Bash removes backslash-newline pairs in unquoted heredocs before checking the delimiter, but this classifier compares physical lines. For example, `tee /tmp/notes.txt <<EOF
EO\
F
if true; then git reset --hard; fi
EOF` terminates Bash's heredoc at the joined `EOF`, making the following `git reset --hard` executable. The classifier instead treats that command as body text until the final literal `EOF`. Its segment scanner drops `then git reset --hard` because the command word is `then`, removing the destructive operation before the fence checks it. This bypasses the default destructive-command guard. Apply Bash's continuation folding when locating unquoted heredoc terminators, or fall back to the full scan whenever such continuations occur.

findings.description: The new `sanctioned_marker` path grants an allow in every mode (including `deny`) when `.run/implement-active.json` holds `{skill: implement|bug, sprint, started_at}` with a `started_at` under two hours old. Nothing authenticates the marker: it is a plain JSON file whose only freshness check is a self-reported timestamp. The trust-input guard added on line 340 only intercepts the Write/Edit/MultiEdit tools, so the same agent whose App Zone writes the fence is meant to gate can create or refresh the marker through the Bash tool, or simply invoke `run-checkpoint.sh mark` itself, and thereby convert the deny-mode fence into an allow for the rest of the session. The pre-existing RUNNING-cache heuristic had the same forgeability, but this change adds a second, cheaper, longer-lived self-attestation and documents deny mode as 'a fence', which it is not while the marker is agent-writable.
findings.failure_mode: An agent (or a prompt-injected agent) outside an implementation run writes a fresh marker via Bash, then every App Zone write is allowed with audit decision `sanctioned_marker`, defeating `implement_gate.mode: deny` and `telemetry` accounting.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not treat a bare JSON file as a sanction. Have `run-checkpoint.sh mark` write the marker through the signed `audit_emit_signed` chain (or include an HMAC over skill|sprint|started_at keyed from a secret the hook can read but the Bash tool cannot), verify the signature in `check_implement_marker`, and extend the Bash hook (`block-destructive-bash.sh`) to refuse writes to `.run/implement-active.json` and the other trust inputs. At minimum, make the marker sanction inactive under `mode: deny` and log it as a tightening-only signal.

findings.description: `LOA_IMPLEMENT_GATE_OVERRIDE=1` in the hook's environment sanctions every App Zone write in every mode, including `deny`, with no additional confirmation. The same PR adds, in `block-destructive-bash.sh`, the explicit invariant that 'an environment variable can never switch the fence off', so the two fences now disagree. Hook environment is inherited from the Claude Code process and can be influenced by `.claude/settings*.json` `env` blocks, `.envrc`, or shell rc files that other tooling writes; none of those paths are in the trust-input list on line 340.
findings.failure_mode: An override variable set once (by an operator for a one-off, or injected via a settings/env file write) silently neutralises the gate for all subsequent sessions, with only an `override` audit row as evidence.
findings.suggested_fix: Scope the override: require it to be accompanied by a short-lived, operator-created file (or a one-time token) rather than a bare env var, ignore it under `mode: deny`, and emit an `ask` with an explicit reason instead of a silent allow. Add `.claude/settings*.json` and `.envrc` to the trust-input list, or document why env-sourced override is acceptable while the Bash fence forbids it.

findings.description: `load_gate_config` returns silently with `gate_mode=ask` when `yq` or `jq` is missing, when `.loa.config.yaml` is absent, or when both yq invocations fail to parse it. An operator who has opted into `implement_gate.mode: deny` therefore gets the weaker `ask` behaviour with no audit row recording the downgrade. Because `.loa.config.yaml` is only protected from Write/Edit (line 340), a Bash-driven edit that makes the file unparseable (or a tooling change that removes yq from PATH) is enough to drop the fence from deny to ask.
findings.failure_mode: Deny mode is silently downgraded to ask on any config-read failure; the only way to notice is to run `--effective-mode` manually.
findings.suggested_fix: Treat a configured-but-unreadable mode as fail-closed for the fence: if the config file exists and cannot be parsed, or the tooling is missing, emit an `ask` with reason `config unreadable` and write a `compliance.mode.fallback` row (the fallback-row pattern already exists for the claims modifier). Consider caching the last good mode in a lead-owned file so a transient parse error does not change behaviour.

findings.description: The per-segment body scan for `nonexec` heredocs only keeps a segment when its first word, after wrapper stripping, is a fence verb. `_bdb_hd_segword` strips sudo/env/command-style wrappers, assignments, quotes and absolute paths, but not shell keywords (`then`, `do`, `else`, `elif`, `function`, `alias`, `trap`, `export`, `local`, `return`). A body line such as an if/then or for/do block whose destructive verb follows the keyword is therefore dropped, whereas the pre-change full-text scan matched the verb anywhere in the body. Separately, `_bdb_hd_same_line_exec` decides whether the written target is executed later in the same command by exact basename equality against each token; a reference to the target through a glob, bracket expression, or substitution on a later line is not equal to the basename and so is not recognised, while that later line is not re-checked by `_bdb_hd_ctx_bad`. Together these let a body that the old scan would have flagged be written and executed within one command without the fence seeing the verb.
findings.failure_mode: A destructive command nested under a shell keyword inside a heredoc body written to a plain-looking path, and executed later in the same Bash invocation via an indirect reference to the file, is no longer matched by the fence rules; this is a coverage regression relative to the #1245-era full scan.
findings.suggested_fix: In `_bdb_hd_segword`, treat shell reserved words (`if then else elif fi do done while until for case esac function select time coproc` and `alias trap export local declare typeset readonly return`) as strippable prefixes, or mark any segment that begins with a keyword as `_hd_full=1`. In `_bdb_hd_same_line_exec`, fail closed when a later line contains `$(`, backticks, process substitution, or any glob/bracket character adjacent to a path token, and treat a non-literal argument to a non-safe-reader command as a possible reference to the target. Add corpus entries for keyword-prefixed bodies and indirect execution references.

findings.description: `_bdb_hd_exec_dest` decides that a write target is 'executable content' using `_bdb_hd_re_ext`, `_bdb_hd_re_sys`, `_bdb_hd_re_rc`, `/etc`, bin dirs and PATH dirs. Common auto-sourced or auto-executed locations are missing: `~/.bash_aliases` and `~/.bash_completion` (sourced by default Debian/Ubuntu bashrc), `~/.config/autostart/*.desktop`, `~/.config/systemd/user/*.service`, `~/.ssh/config` (ProxyCommand/LocalCommand), `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`, `.claude/commands/`, `.claude/agents/`, `CLAUDE.md` and other agent instruction files, `.github/workflows/`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `Makefile`, `package.json` scripts, `.vimrc`/`.tmux.conf`. A heredoc appended to any of these is classified `nonexec`, so everything in the body except fence-verb-led segments is removed from the scan, and PATH-directory matching is by string equality so a relative path containing `..` or a symlinked directory is not recognised as a PATH dir.
findings.failure_mode: Content written to an unlisted persistence location (an alias definition, a function body, a workflow step) that contains a destructive command not at segment start is no longer flagged by the fence, and it will execute at a later shell start or CI run rather than within the guarded command.
findings.suggested_fix: Extend `_bdb_hd_re_rc`/`_bdb_hd_re_sys` with the locations above, treat any path under `.claude/`, `.github/`, `.ssh/`, `.config/` and any hidden dotfile in `$HOME` as executable content, and canonicalise the destination directory (resolve `..` components and, where available, `realpath -m`) before comparing with PATH entries. Keep the Write-tool parity note in the header accurate by listing which locations the Write tool also fails to fence.

findings.cross_file_justification: profiles.yaml (new, lines 40-41) sets guardrails.input.enabled and guardrails.danger_level.enforce to false in the `standard` profile that applies when loa.profile is unset or unknown; danger-level-enforcer.sh (diff) replaces its `// true` default with `loa_knob ... false`, so the effective default flips from enforce-on to enforce-off.
findings.description: Before this change `is_enforcement_enabled` defaulted to true when the config file was missing or the key was unset. It now sources `profile-lib.sh` without any error handling and calls `loa_knob guardrails.danger_level.enforce false`; the `standard` profile (the implicit default for an unset or unknown `loa.profile`) sets that key to false, and the caller fallback is also false. The same profile disables `guardrails.input.enabled`, so the pre-execution guardrails prelude in `input_guardrails.md` is skipped unless a repo explicitly opts in. The net effect is that both guardrail layers are off by default for every repository that does not pin `loa.profile: full` or set the keys explicitly, and any failure to load the profile library yields 'disabled' rather than 'enabled'.
findings.failure_mode: Repositories upgrading to this release silently lose danger-level enforcement and input guardrails unless they edit `.loa.config.yaml`; a missing or broken `profile-lib.sh` also disables enforcement instead of failing safe.
findings.suggested_fix: Keep the enforcer fail-closed: pass `true` as the caller fallback, guard the `source` so a missing library leaves enforcement on, and log a WARN when the effective value comes from a profile rather than an explicit key. Reconsider whether the two guardrail keys belong in `standard` at false; if the migration (D-4.4/DEC-0161) requires it, emit a one-time session-start notice so operators know enforcement is off.

findings.cross_file_justification: constraints.json removes C-TEAM-001..005 and CLAUDE.loa.md drops the generated Agent Teams table; the removed C-TEAM-005 text was the instruction-layer statement that teammates MUST NOT modify .claude/ and claimed enforcement by a PreToolUse Write/Edit hook. agent-teams-reference.md and hooks-reference.md are listed as changed but were truncated from the review, so whether the mechanical hook (team-skill-guard.sh / System Zone guard) survives cannot be confirmed from the diff.
findings.description: The PR deletes all five agent-team constraints, including the System Zone read-only rule (C-TEAM-005, severity critical, sourced from a prior security review) and the lead-only `.run/` state-file rule (C-TEAM-003). These were the model-facing instructions that complement the mechanical hooks; C-TEAM-003 in particular is what told teammates not to write the very files (`sprint-plan-state.json`, `implement-active.json`) that `implement-gate.sh` treats as sanctions. With the prose gone, a teammate that is prompt-injected or simply confused has no instruction-layer barrier, and if the referenced hook was also retired in the truncated files the only remaining control is the implement-gate trust-input ask, which does not cover Bash.
findings.failure_mode: A teammate agent modifies `.claude/hooks/` or `.run/` state files, altering fence behaviour or sanctioning its own App Zone writes for every agent in the team; the removed constraints were the documented mitigation for incident #337 and PR 341.
findings.suggested_fix: Confirm the mechanical enforcement (team-skill-guard.sh and the System Zone PreToolUse guard) still exists and is registered; if so, keep a one-line pointer in CLAUDE.loa.md to it. Otherwise restore at least C-TEAM-003 and C-TEAM-005 (or fold them into the floor in `.claude/data/floor.yaml`) so the invariant is both instructed and enforced, and have the Bash fence refuse writes under `.claude/hooks/` and `.run/` for non-lead sessions (`LOA_TEAM_MEMBER` set).

findings.description: `_bdb_hd_is_safe_reader` lists `git`, `gh`, `br`, `jq`, `yq`, `mkdir` and `touch` as commands that may name a heredoc's target without making the heredoc interpreter-class. `git` can consume the target as a patch (`apply`, `am`) that writes into hook or config paths, `jq -f`/`yq --from-file` evaluate the target as a program, and `gh` can post it externally. These are not pure readers; the allowlist is wider than its comment implies.
findings.failure_mode: A heredoc body written to a plain file and then fed to one of these 'safe readers' in the same command escapes the full scan even though the reader can turn the content into further writes or evaluation.
findings.suggested_fix: Narrow the safe-reader list to genuine read-only tools (`cat ls wc head tail grep rg diff cmp stat file test [ echo printf sort uniq *sum`) and treat `git`, `gh`, `br`, `jq`, `yq` references to the target as interpreter-class unless the subcommand is in an explicit read-only set (`git diff|log|show|status`).

findings.description: `LOA_AUDIT_REPLAY=1` in the hook environment adds `replay: true` to every audit row this gate writes, including live `deny`, `ask` and `sanctioned_*` decisions. If the register or any consumer discounts replay rows (the stated purpose of DEC-0167), a stray or injected environment variable causes real decisions to be excluded from accounting without any marker that the flag was active.
findings.failure_mode: Live gate decisions are tagged as replay and dropped from compliance counts, hiding unsanctioned App Zone writes from review.
findings.suggested_fix: Require replay mode to be explicitly requested per invocation (a CLI flag on the replay tool) rather than inherited from the hook's environment, or write a separate `compliance.replay_mode` row at hook start so consumers can detect when the flag was set in a live session.
